introduction.p: A bounded function has a Riemann integral when its upper and lower sums can be made arbitrarily close. This section uses that criterion to establish integrability for continuous functions, monotone functions, and bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities. Boundedness alone is insufficient.

subsection.p: This criterion is the cleanest way to understand which functions are integrable. It says that the integral exists when the remaining uncertainty can be squeezed down to zero.

exercise.title: Why is the upper-lower test the existence test for Riemann integrals?

statement.p: A bounded function is integrable when upper sums and lower sums can be forced together. In your own words, why does that squeezing criterion decide existence, and why is it the same idea that first appeared as area trapped between overestimates and underestimates?

hint.p: If upper and lower sums can be made arbitrarily close, their limiting values agree and determine a unique integral.

subsection.title: Continuous functions are integrable
subsection.p: A continuous graph on a closed interval cannot jump. If we look at a short enough piece of the graph, the output values stay close together.
That is exactly what the upper-lower test needs.

statement.p: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].

paragraphs.title: Proof idea
paragraphs.p: A continuous function on a closed interval has a special kind of steadiness:

p.me: \text{if }x\text{ and }y\text{ are close enough, then }f(x)\text{ and }f(y)\text{ are close,}

paragraphs.p: and the same meaning of “close enough” works everywhere on the interval. This property is called uniform continuity. To see why it follows here, suppose it failed for some fixed output gap \eta>0. Bisect the closed interval repeatedly, each time retaining a half that still contains pairs of arbitrarily close inputs with output gap at least \eta. Such a half must exist: otherwise the two halves have distance thresholds, and continuity at their common endpoint also controls pairs straddling it. The retained intervals are nested and their lengths tend to zero, so completeness gives a common point c. Eventually a retained interval lies wholly in a neighborhood of c where continuity makes every value differ from f(c) by less than \eta/2. No two values there can have gap at least \eta, a contradiction.

exercise.title: Why are continuous functions on a closed interval integrable?

statement.p: Continuity on [a,b] keeps oscillation small on small subintervals. In your own words, why does that force upper and lower sums together, and why does the closed bounded interval matter for that argument?

hint.p: On a closed interval a continuous function cannot jump wildly inside tiny pieces. Small intervals have small oscillation, so the upper-lower gap can be made small.

subsection.title: Monotone functions are integrable
subsection.p: Continuity is enough for integrability, but it is not necessary.

A function may jump and still be integrable. The simplest reason is monotonicity: a monotone function can move only one way. It may jump, but it cannot oscillate up and down forever inside every small interval.

subsection.p: This theorem explains why jumps are not automatically dangerous. A step function can be monotone, and a monotone step function is integrable.

subsection.title: Functions with finitely many jump discontinuities
subsection.p: A function may have several jumps and still be integrable. The reason is the same: finitely many points can be covered by intervals whose total width is as small as we wish.

statement.p: If f is bounded on [a,b] and is continuous except at finitely many points, then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].

paragraphs.title: Proof idea
paragraphs.p: Suppose the discontinuities occur at finitely many points. Put tiny intervals around those points. Since there are only finitely many of them, we can make the total width of all the tiny intervals very small.
On those tiny intervals, the function may behave badly, but it is bounded. So the upper-lower contribution is at worst
which can be made small.
On the rest of the interval, the function is continuous on closed pieces. So the upper-lower contribution there can also be made small.
Putting the two parts together, the total upper-lower gap can be made smaller than any chosen \varepsilon. Hence the function is integrable.

exercise.title: Why can finitely many jumps still leave a function integrable?

statement.p: A step function is integrable, and changing finitely many values does not change a Riemann integral. In your own words, why does a jump at one point (or at finitely many points) fail to disturb the accumulated area, and why is a monotone function similarly safe?

hint.p: A discontinuity can be covered by a tiny interval whose contribution is negligible. The height at one point cannot change accumulated area.

note.title: Changing finitely many values does not change a Riemann integral
note.p: If two bounded functions differ only at finitely many points, then either both are integrable with the same integral, or neither is integrable.

note.p: The following functions are Riemann integrable on closed intervals:

The general rule. The ultimate test for Riemann integrability was proven by Henri Lebesgue. A bounded function is integrable if and only if its set of discontinuity points has measure zero---meaning that, for every \varepsilon>0, those points can be covered by a finite or countable collection of open intervals whose lengths sum to less than \varepsilon. This criterion is stated here for perspective; its proof requires a later course in analysis.

subsection.p: The integral is now on solid ground. We know what it means, how to estimate it, what signs do, what algebraic rules it obeys, and which common functions actually have one.
The next chapter studies accumulation functions with a moving endpoint. For a continuous integrand, differentiating the accumulation recovers the integrand.

exercise.title: Why is boundedness not enough for Riemann integrability?

statement.p: The function that is 1 on rationals and 0 on irrationals is bounded on [0,1] but not Riemann integrable. In your own words, why do upper and lower sums stay apart on every partition, and what does that example show about saying bounded functions have area?

hint.p: Every interval, no matter how short, contains both rationals and irrationals. So every lower sum is 0 and every upper sum is the length of the interval.
